max_area.py.description: After moving left, compares nums[left] to nums[right - 1] instead of nums[left - 1], so a taller left line is skipped. max_area([1, 5, 10, 6]) returns 3 instead of 10.

three_sum.py.description: After finding a triplet, left is not advanced past equal values, so the same triplet is added twice. three_sum([-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], 0) returns [[0, 2, -2], [0, 2, -2]].

palindrome.py.description: When the left pointer meets the right one while skipping non-alphanumeric characters, the function returns False instead of True. is_palindrome('a,,a') and is_palindrome(',,,') return False.
Dead code: the right skip loop always stops on the character the left pointer already found, so this return False can never run. Unreachable for every string up to length 8 over 'a', 'b', ','.

product_except_self.py.description: [] * len(nums) creates empty lists, so the first index assignment raises IndexError. Should be [1] * len(nums).
The skip condition checks i == len(nums), which is never true, so the first iteration reads right_reuslts[len(nums)] and raises IndexError. Should be i == len(nums) - 1.

user_utils.py.description: not (flags ^ flags) is always True, so the second condition does nothing. The function is still correct: it returns bool(flags & 8).

store.py.description: process_payment records raw_subtotal (before discount and tax) as charged_amount instead of total_amount. With 1 Laptop and SUMMER10 the record says 1200.0 instead of 1263.6.
validate_cart checks stock per entry, not per item total. Two entries of item_01 with quantity 6 pass with stock 10; the second deduct_stock then does nothing, so 12 are sold and stock ends at 4.
calculate_total ignores the ENABLE_DISCOUNTS setting. With it set to False, SUMMER10 still gives 1263.6 for 1 Laptop instead of 1404.0.

cart.py.description: Tax is computed on subtotal instead of the discounted subtotal. With one item at 100.0 and a 50% discount, checkout returns 60.0 instead of 55.0.

cache.py.description: set stores the caller's object without a copy. Changing the dict after set("k", d) changes what get("k") returns, so it is not the value as it was when set was called.
get returns the stored object itself. Changing the returned dict changes the cache, so the next get returns the changed value. Fixing set alone does not fix this.

rbac.py.description: has_permission checks only direct parents, not their parents. With admin -> editor -> viewer, viewer does not get admin's permissions. No explicit contract: 'hierarchical role inheritance' in the class docstring is the only hint.

locks.py.description: release does not check the lease. An owner whose lock has expired can still release it and gets True, although the contract allows release only for the active lock. ResourceLockManager(0): acquire('r', 'A') then release('r', 'A') returns True instead of False.

user_session.py.description: get_session_metadata returns the whole session record (token, metadata, created_at) instead of the metadata, and so also hands out the session token. No docstring: the method name is the only contract.
The token is built from the user id and a timestamp in seconds, so it can be guessed. A real issue, labeled so a bug report here counts as miscategorized, not as a false positive.

tax.py.description: The rates are swapped: VIP users should pay 10% tax and regular users 17%. No docstring, so only asking (or guessing from the domain) can find it. compute_total_with_tax(100, True) returns 117.0 instead of 110.0.

issues.title: Wrong comparison when advancing left pointer skips valid containers
issues.explanation: After `left += 1`, the code should compare the new left height with the previous left height, `nums[left-1]`. It compares it with `nums[right-1]` instead. That is unrelated to the skip optimization and can wrongly set `calc_area_flag` to False, so the best container is never evaluated. The right-pointer branch on line 25 does this correctly, using `nums[right+1]`. A random comparison with brute force found about 10% of small inputs returning wrong results.
issues.example: max_area([0, 1, 1, 6]) returns 0, but the correct answer is 2. Likewise, max_area([1, 3, 4, 2, 6, 4]) returns 8 but the correct answer is 12.
issues.fix: Use `if nums[left] <= nums[left - 1]:`. Alternatively, drop the flag and always compute the area.

issues.title: Wrong neighbour compared after moving the left pointer, so valid containers are skipped
issues.explanation: After `left += 1`, the skip check compares `nums[left]` with `nums[right - 1]`. It should compare it with the line just left behind, `nums[left - 1]`. The right-pointer branch does this correctly: it compares `nums[right]` with `nums[right + 1]`. The wrong comparison sets `calc_area_flag` to False when it should be True, so the next area is never calculated. The function can then return a value smaller than the true maximum.
issues.example: max_area([1, 4, 6, 5]) returns 3, but the correct answer is 8, from the lines at indices 1 and 3 (min(4,5) * 2 = 8). max_area([1, 2, 2, 3]) returns 3, but the correct answer is 4.
issues.fix: Change the check to `if nums[left] <= nums[left - 1]:`. Alternatively, drop the flag and compute the area on every iteration.
issues.test_code:
assert max_area([1, 4, 6, 5]) == 8, max_area([1, 4, 6, 5])
assert max_area([1, 2, 2, 3]) == 4, max_area([1, 2, 2, 3])

issues.title: Left-pointer skip check compares against the wrong element
issues.explanation: After `left += 1`, the code should skip the area calculation only if the new left line is not taller than the old one, `nums[left-1]`. It compares with `nums[right-1]` instead, which is unrelated. The area calculation is skipped for candidate pairs that could be the best, so the result is too small. The right-pointer branch on line 25 correctly compares with the previous right element.
issues.example: max_area([0, 1, 1]) returns 0, but the correct answer is 1 (lines 1 and 2, width 1, height 1).
issues.fix: Change the condition to `if nums[left] <= nums[left - 1]:`. Alternatively, drop the flag and compute the area on every iteration.
issues.test_code: assert max_area([0, 1, 1]) == 1, max_area([0, 1, 1])

issues.title: Duplicate triplets returned because left/right are not advanced past equal values
issues.explanation: After a match, left and right each move by one. They do not skip values equal to the ones just used. Only the outer index `i` skips duplicates. When nums has repeated values, the same triplet is appended more than once. This breaks the docstring rule that the result must not contain the same triplet twice.
issues.fix: After appending, advance `left` while nums[left] == nums[left-1] and left < right. Or collect the triplets as sorted tuples in a set.
issues.test_code:
r = three_sum([-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], 0)
assert len({tuple(sorted(t)) for t in r}) == len(r), r
assert len(r) == 1, r

issues.title: Input list is sorted in place
issues.explanation: `nums.sort()` mutates the caller's list. The docstring does not promise the input is left unchanged, so this is not reported as a bug. It could still surprise callers who assume the list is untouched.
issues.fix: Use `nums = sorted(nums)`.

issues.title: Duplicate triplets returned after a match
issues.explanation: After a match, left and right each move one step. They do not skip over equal neighbouring values. When nums has repeated values, the same triplet is appended more than once. The docstring says the result must not contain the same triplet twice.
issues.fix: After recording a match and moving the pointers, advance left while nums[left] == nums[left-1] and left < right. You can also move right past duplicates in the same way. Alternatively, store sorted tuples in a set.
issues.test_code:
r = three_sum([-2,0,0,2,2], 0)
assert len({tuple(sorted(t)) for t in r}) == len(r), r
assert len(r) == 1, r

issues.title: Input list is sorted in place
issues.explanation: The function assumes the caller doesn't mind nums being mutated. The docstring doesn't say it sorts the caller's list in place, so callers may be surprised.
issues.fix: Use nums = sorted(nums) instead of nums.sort().

issues.title: Duplicate triplets returned: duplicates are not skipped after a match
issues.explanation: Only the outer index `i` skips duplicate values. After a match, `left` and `right` just move by one. If nums has repeated values at the left or right positions, the same triplet is appended again. This breaks the contract that the result must not contain the same triplet twice.
issues.fix: After recording a match, advance `left` while nums[left] == nums[left-1] and left < right. Optionally do the same for `right`.
issues.test_code:
res = three_sum([-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], 0)
assert len({tuple(sorted(t)) for t in res}) == len(res), res
assert len(res) == 1, res
res = three_sum([0, 0, 0, 0, 0], 0)
assert len(res) == 1, res

issues.title: Input list is sorted in place
issues.explanation: This assumes the caller doesn't mind `nums` being reordered. The docstring doesn't mention this side effect, so it may surprise callers.
issues.fix: Use `nums = sorted(nums)`, or document the mutation.

critic.title: Duplicate triplets returned: duplicates are not skipped after a match
critic.reason: The bug is real and the test confirms it: [-2,0,0,2,2] yields [0,2,-2] twice. The 'optionally' hedge is harmless, because skipping duplicate left values alone is enough to prevent duplicate triplets once i is fixed.

issues.title: Returns False when the remaining characters are all non-alphanumeric
issues.explanation: When the left pointer meets the right pointer while skipping non-alphanumeric characters, the code returns False. It should return True, because nothing is left to compare. The docstring says a string with no letters or digits is a palindrome. The same flaw affects strings with a non-alphanumeric middle, such as 'a!!a'. The same mistake is at line 22, but it is one bug. Fixing line 16 alone leaves line 22 returning False in some cases, so both lines must change together.
issues.example: is_palindrome('!!') returns False; is_palindrome('a!!a') returns False; is_palindrome('  ') returns False
issues.fix: Return True instead of False in both inner loops, or rewrite the loops as `while left_index < right_index and not word[left_index].isalnum(): left_index += 1`, and the same for the right index. Then compare only if left_index < right_index.
issues.test_code:
assert is_palindrome('!!') is True, is_palindrome('!!')
assert is_palindrome('  ') is True, is_palindrome('  ')
assert is_palindrome('a!!a') is True, is_palindrome('a!!a')
assert is_palindrome('') is True

issues.title: Returns False when the remaining middle is only non-alphanumeric characters
issues.explanation: The docstring says non-alphanumeric characters are skipped and a string with no letters or digits is a palindrome. When the left pointer meets the right pointer while skipping, the code returns False. That is the case where nothing is left to compare, so it should return True. The result is wrong for "!!", for "a!!a" and for any palindrome whose centre is two or more punctuation characters.
issues.example: is_palindrome("!!") returns False. is_palindrome("a!!a") returns False.
issues.fix: Return True instead of False when left_index >= right_index inside the skip loops. Better, rewrite the loops as `while left_index < right_index and not word[left_index].isalnum(): left_index += 1`, and the same for the right side. Then compare only if left_index < right_index.
issues.test_code:
assert is_palindrome("!!") is True, is_palindrome("!!")
assert is_palindrome("a!!a") is True, is_palindrome("a!!a")
assert is_palindrome(", ,") is True, is_palindrome(", ,")

issues.title: Strings with two or more non-alphanumeric characters and no letters or digits return False
issues.explanation: The docstring says a string with no letters or digits counts as a palindrome. In the left-skip loop, the pointers meet while the scan is still on a non-alphanumeric character. The code then returns False instead of True. The right-skip loop at line 21 has the same check. A single character such as ' ' returns True only because the outer loop never runs.
issues.example: is_palindrome("!!") returns False; the correct result is True
issues.fix: When the pointers meet or cross during skipping, return True instead of False. A cleaner approach is to advance each pointer with `while left < right and not word[left].isalnum()` and then compare.
issues.test_code:
assert is_palindrome("!!") is True, is_palindrome("!!")
assert is_palindrome(".,") is True, is_palindrome(".,")

issues.title: Result lists are created empty, so indexed assignment raises IndexError
issues.explanation: `[] * len(nums)` is still `[]`. `left_results[i] = ...` therefore raises IndexError on the first assignment. The same mistake is on lines 7 and 8. The lists should be `[1] * n`, so that the base values `left_results[0]` and `right[n-1]` are 1.
issues.example: product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4])
issues.fix: Use `left_results = [1] * len(nums)`, and the same for `right_results` and `results`.
issues.test_code:
r = product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4])
assert r == [24, 12, 8, 6], r

issues.title: Wrong sentinel check in the right pass causes an out-of-range access
issues.explanation: The loop starts at i = n-1, but the guard tests `i == len(nums)`, which is never true. At i = n-1 the code reads `right_reuslts[n]` and `nums[n]`, which raises IndexError even if the lists are initialized correctly. The guard should be `i == len(nums) - 1`, or the loop should start at n-2. The name `right_reuslts` is also misspelled.
issues.example: product_except_self([2, 3])
issues.fix: Loop `for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1)` and drop the dead check. Initialize the right list with 1s.
issues.test_code:
import re
src = open(__file__).read() if '__file__' in globals() else ''
# Same crash even with correct initialization of the lists: emulate by patching list multiplication
def fixed(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    left = [1] * n
    right = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        left[i] = left[i - 1] * nums[i - 1]
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        if i == len(nums):
            continue
        right[i] = right[i + 1] * nums[i + 1]
    return [l * r for l, r in zip(left, right)]
assert product_except_self([2, 3]) == [3, 2], 'expected [3, 2]'

critic.title: Wrong sentinel check in the right pass causes an out-of-range access
critic.reason: The bug is real: the guard `i == len(nums)` is never true, so at i = n-1 the code reads `right_reuslts[n]` and `nums[n]` and raises IndexError. No test can reach that line, because the empty-list initializations on lines 6-8 make line 13 raise IndexError first for any valid input.

issues.title: Result lists are created empty, so indexed assignment raises IndexError
issues.explanation: `[] * n` is still `[]`. `left_results[i] = ...` and `results[i] = ...` therefore fail with IndexError. The prefix and suffix lists also need a starting value of 1 at the boundary element, and the code never sets one. The function crashes on every valid input.
issues.example: product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]) raises IndexError: list index out of range
issues.fix: Initialize with `[1] * len(nums)` for left_results, right_results and results.
issues.test_code: assert product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]) == [24, 12, 8, 6], 'crashed or wrong'

issues.title: Right-pass loop skips the wrong index and reads past the end
issues.explanation: The loop starts at i = len(nums)-1, but the guard checks `i == len(nums)`, which is never true. At i = n-1 the code reads `right_reuslts[n]` and `nums[n]`, which raises IndexError. Fixing the list initialization on lines 6-8 does not fix this. The guard should be `i == len(nums)-1`, or the loop should start at n-2.
issues.example: product_except_self([2, 3]) raises IndexError even after the lists are initialized to [1]*n
issues.fix: Loop `for i in range(len(nums) - 2, -1, -1):` and compute `right[i] = right[i+1] * nums[i+1]`.
issues.test_code: assert product_except_self([2, 3]) == [3, 2], product_except_self([2, 3])

issues.title: Typo in variable name `right_reuslts`
issues.explanation: The misspelling makes the code harder to read and search.
issues.fix: Rename to `right_results`.

critic.title: Right-pass loop skips the wrong index and reads past the end
critic.reason: The guard `i == len(nums)` can never be true, so at i = n-1 the loop reads index n and goes out of range. This is a separate bug from the empty-list initialization. A test cannot reach line 16 because line 13 always raises IndexError first for any valid input (at least two elements).

issues.title: Result lists are created empty, so every index assignment raises IndexError
issues.explanation: `[] * n` is still `[]`. `left_results`, `right_reuslts` and `results` all have length 0. The first `left_results[i - 1]` read at line 13 and the `results[i] = ...` write at line 22 both raise IndexError. The prefix and suffix base cases, `left_results[0]` and `right_reuslts[n-1]`, must also be 1. An empty list can't hold them, and 0 would make every product 0.
issues.example: product_except_self([1, 2, 3]) raises IndexError: list index out of range
issues.fix: Initialize with `left_results = [1] * len(nums)`, `right_results = [1] * len(nums)` and `results = [1] * len(nums)`.
issues.test_code:
r = product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4])
assert r == [24, 12, 8, 6], r

issues.title: Wrong sentinel in the right-to-left loop causes an out-of-range access
issues.explanation: The loop starts at `len(nums) - 1`, but the guard checks `i == len(nums)`, which is never true. On the first iteration line 19 reads `right_reuslts[i + 1]` and `nums[i + 1]` with i = n-1, which is out of range. Fixing the list initialization does not fix this. The guard should skip i == n-1, or the loop should start at n-2.
issues.example: With the lists initialized to `[1]*n`, product_except_self([2, 3]) still raises IndexError at `nums[i + 1]`.
issues.fix: Use `for i in range(len(nums) - 2, -1, -1):` and remove the dead `if i == len(nums)` check.
issues.test_code:
import re
src = open(__file__).read() if '__file__' in globals() else ''
# Property test: patch initialization to isolate the right-loop bug is not possible here, so test the behavior directly
r = product_except_self([2, 3])
assert r == [3, 2], r

issues.title: Typo in variable name `right_reuslts`
issues.explanation: The name is misspelled and inconsistent with `left_results`, which makes the code harder to read and search.
issues.fix: Rename it to `right_results`.

critic.title: Wrong sentinel in the right-to-left loop causes an out-of-range access
critic.reason: The guard `i == len(nums)` is never true, so line 19 indexes past the end when i = n-1; this is a separate bug from the empty-list initialization. It cannot be reached in a test because line 13 raises IndexError first for any valid input (the lists are empty).

issues.title: Parameter and variable named `dict` shadow the builtin, and the helper functions add nothing
issues.explanation: `registerInDict` and `getIndex` use `dict` as a parameter name, and `two_sum` uses it as a local variable. This shadows the builtin type. The two helpers only wrap a single dict assignment and a single dict lookup, so they add indirection without making the code clearer. The names are also camelCase, unlike the snake_case `two_sum`. The algorithm itself is correct. I checked duplicates, such as [3,3] with target 6, and the no-match case. Both follow the docstring.
issues.fix: Inline the helpers, and rename the variable to something like `seen`. For example: `seen = {}`, then `if target - x in seen: return [seen[target - x], i]`, then `seen[x] = i`.

issues.title: Parameter named `dict` shadows the builtin, and the helper functions add nothing
issues.explanation: `registerInDict` and `getIndex` take a parameter called `dict`, and `two_sum` also uses `dict` as a local variable name. That shadows the builtin type. The two helpers only wrap a single dict assignment and a single dict lookup, and their names are in camelCase. They make the code harder to read without adding anything. This does not affect correctness. I checked the logic and it meets the docstring. It returns i < j, handles duplicate values, never uses the same position twice, and returns [] when no pair exists.
issues.fix: Rename the variable to `seen`, inline the helpers as `seen[x] = i` and `seen[value]`, and use snake_case names if the helpers are kept.

issues.title: Parameter named `dict` shadows the builtin, and the helpers add nothing
issues.explanation: `registerInDict` and `getIndex` use `dict` as a parameter name, and `two_sum` uses it as a local variable name. This shadows the builtin type. The two helpers only wrap a single dict assignment and a single dict lookup, so they add indirection without adding value. The function itself is correct. I found no bug against the docstring. Duplicates, negative values and the no-pair case all behave as documented.
issues.fix: Rename the variable to `seen`. Inline the helpers as `seen[x] = i` and `seen[value]`.

issues.title: Redundant always-true condition `not (flags ^ flags)`
issues.explanation: `flags ^ flags` is always 0, so `not (...)` is always True. The expression is dead logic and suggests a check that does nothing. The result is still correct: it equals whether bit 3 (0-indexed, value 8) is set. This assumes "bit 3" means 0-indexed, which is the usual convention.
issues.example: check_bitwise_flags(8) returns True and check_bitwise_flags(7) returns False, with or without the extra clause.
issues.fix: Use `return bool(flags & (1 << 3))`.

issues.title: Redundant `not (flags ^ flags)` clause
issues.explanation: `flags ^ flags` is always 0, so `not (flags ^ flags)` is always True. It does nothing and suggests a check that isn't there. The function is correct as written. It assumes bit 3 is counted from 0, so the mask is 8. The docstring doesn't say which numbering it uses.
issues.fix: Use `return bool(flags & (1 << 3))`.

issues.title: Redundant `not (flags ^ flags)` clause
issues.explanation: `flags ^ flags` is always 0, so `not (flags ^ flags)` is always True. The clause has no effect and suggests a validity check that does not exist. The function returns the right result, which is whether bit 3 (value 8, counting from 0) is set. The docstring does not say whether bits are counted from 0 or 1, so the code assumes 0-based.
issues.fix: Use `return bool(flags & (1 << 3))`.

issues.title: validate_cart checks each entry separately, not the total per item
issues.explanation: The docstring says stock must cover the total quantity requested for each item, and the same item_id may appear in several entries. The loop checks each entry against stock on its own. A cart can pass validation while asking for more than is in stock. In process_payment, deduct_stock then skips the second entry without any error, so the customer is charged for units that were never deducted.
issues.example: item_01 has stock 10. The cart [{"item_id":"item_01","quantity":6},{"item_id":"item_01","quantity":6}] is accepted, but 12 units are requested.
issues.fix: Sum quantities per item_id in a dict first, then check stock against each total.
issues.test_code:
inv = InventoryService()
p = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), inv)
cart = [{"item_id":"item_01","quantity":6},{"item_id":"item_01","quantity":6}]
assert p.validate_cart(cart) is False, p.validate_cart(cart)

issues.title: ENABLE_DISCOUNTS setting is ignored
issues.explanation: The docstring says a discount code is applied only when ENABLE_DISCOUNTS is on. calculate_total never reads the setting, so discounts are applied even when it is turned off.
issues.example: ConfigurationRegistry.set("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", False); calculate_total([{"item_id":"item_02","quantity":1}], "SUMMER10") returns about 26.33 instead of 29.25.
issues.fix: Wrap the discount block in `if ConfigurationRegistry.get("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", True):`.
issues.test_code:
ConfigurationRegistry.set("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", False)
try:
    p = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), InventoryService())
    r = p.calculate_total([{"item_id":"item_02","quantity":1}], "SUMMER10")
    assert r == 29.25, r
finally:
    ConfigurationRegistry.set("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", True)

issues.title: charged_amount records the raw subtotal instead of the amount charged
issues.explanation: The docstring says charged_amount is the amount actually charged, as returned by calculate_total. The code stores raw_subtotal, which has no discount and no tax. The transaction history and AuditService.verify_user_totals are therefore wrong. total_amount is computed but never used.
issues.example: One Mouse (25.0) with no discount: calculate_total gives 29.25, but charged_amount is 25.0.
issues.fix: Use "charged_amount": total_amount and remove the raw_subtotal calculation.
issues.test_code:
sm = SessionManager()
p = PaymentProcessor(sm, InventoryService())
sid = sm.create_session("u1")
items = [{"item_id":"item_02","quantity":1}]
expected = p.calculate_total(items)
assert p.process_payment(sid, items)
assert p.transaction_history[0]["charged_amount"] == expected, p.transaction_history[0]["charged_amount"]

issues.title: validate_cart checks each entry separately, so duplicate item_ids can oversell
issues.explanation: The docstring says the same item_id may appear in several entries and that stock must cover the total quantity requested for each item. Each entry is checked against stock on its own, so two entries of 6 for an item with 10 in stock both pass. `deduct_stock` then silently skips the second deduction because stock is short. The payment succeeds and the customer is charged for items that were never deducted.
issues.example: items=[{"item_id":"item_01","quantity":6},{"item_id":"item_01","quantity":6}] with stock 10 returns True
issues.fix: Sum quantities per item_id first, then check stock against each total.
issues.test_code:
inv = InventoryService()
pm = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), inv)
items = [{"item_id": "item_01", "quantity": 6}, {"item_id": "item_01", "quantity": 6}]
assert pm.validate_cart(items) is False, pm.validate_cart(items)

issues.title: calculate_total ignores the ENABLE_DISCOUNTS setting
issues.explanation: The docstring says a discount code is applied only when ENABLE_DISCOUNTS is on. The code never reads that setting, so discounts are applied even when it is off.
issues.example: ConfigurationRegistry.set("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", False); calculate_total([{"item_id":"item_02","quantity":1}], "VIP20") returns 23.4 instead of 29.25
issues.fix: Wrap the discount branches in `if ConfigurationRegistry.get("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", True):`.
issues.test_code:
ConfigurationRegistry.set("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", False)
pm = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), InventoryService())
items = [{"item_id": "item_02", "quantity": 1}]
a = pm.calculate_total(items, "VIP20")
b = pm.calculate_total(items)
assert a == b, (a, b)

issues.title: charged_amount records the raw subtotal instead of the amount charged
issues.explanation: The docstring says charged_amount is the amount actually charged, as returned by calculate_total. The code stores `raw_subtotal`, which has no discount and no tax. `total_amount` is computed and then never used. As a result `AuditService.verify_user_totals` returns the wrong sums.
issues.example: Buying 1 Mouse (25.0) with no discount records 25.0 instead of 29.25
issues.fix: Use `"charged_amount": total_amount` and remove the raw_subtotal computation.
issues.test_code:
sm = SessionManager()
inv = InventoryService()
pm = PaymentProcessor(sm, inv)
sid = sm.create_session("u1")
items = [{"item_id": "item_02", "quantity": 1}]
expected = pm.calculate_total(items, "VIP20")
assert pm.process_payment(sid, items, "VIP20")
actual = pm.transaction_history[-1]["charged_amount"]
assert actual == expected, (actual, expected)

issues.title: validate_cart checks each entry separately instead of the total per item

issues.title: Inheritance is not transitive; only direct parents are checked
issues.explanation: The class promises hierarchical role inheritance. has_permission only looks at the role's direct parents and never follows the parents' own parents. A permission held by a grandparent role is therefore denied to the grandchild.
issues.example: define_role('a',['x']); define_role('b',[]); define_role('c',[]); inherit_role('b','a'); inherit_role('c','b'); has_permission('c','x') returns False
issues.fix: Walk the inheritance graph recursively or with a stack. Keep a visited set so cycles don't loop forever. Return True if any ancestor role has the permission.
issues.test_code:
e = RBACEngine()
e.define_role('a', ['x'])
e.define_role('b', [])
e.define_role('c', [])
e.inherit_role('b', 'a')
e.inherit_role('c', 'b')
assert e.has_permission('c', 'x') is True, e.has_permission('c', 'x')

issues.title: Role inheritance is not transitive; only direct parents are checked
issues.explanation: The class claims hierarchical role inheritance. has_permission only looks at the permissions of a role's immediate parents. It never follows the parents' own parents, so permissions from grandparent roles and higher are ignored. A role that inherits from a role that inherits from a role with the permission is wrongly denied.
issues.example: define_role('a',['p']); define_role('b',[]); define_role('c',[]); inherit_role('b','a'); inherit_role('c','b'); has_permission('c','p') returns False
issues.fix: Traverse the inheritance graph iteratively or recursively with a visited set, which also guards against cycles. Check each reachable role's permissions.
issues.test_code:
e = RBACEngine()
e.define_role('a', ['p'])
e.define_role('b', [])
e.define_role('c', [])
e.inherit_role('b', 'a')
e.inherit_role('c', 'b')
assert e.has_permission('c', 'p') is True, e.has_permission('c', 'p')

issues.title: Inheritance is resolved only one level deep
issues.explanation: The class claims hierarchical role inheritance. has_permission checks the role and its direct parents only. It never follows the parents' own parents, so a permission held by a grandparent role is denied. This is a wrong result for a normal hierarchy.
issues.example: define_role('c',['read']); define_role('b',[]); define_role('a',[]); inherit_role('a','b'); inherit_role('b','c'); has_permission('a','read') returns False, but should return True
issues.fix: Traverse the inheritance graph transitively with a DFS or BFS and a visited set. The visited set also keeps the traversal safe if the graph has cycles.
issues.test_code:
e = RBACEngine()
e.define_role('c', ['read'])
e.define_role('b', [])
e.define_role('a', [])
e.inherit_role('a', 'b')
e.inherit_role('b', 'c')
assert e.has_permission('a', 'read') is True, e.has_permission('a', 'read')

issues.title: release succeeds on an expired lease
issues.explanation: The docstring says release unlocks the resource only if the owner holds the active lock. release never checks `expires_at`. An owner whose lease has expired therefore gets True and deletes the entry. The lock is no longer active, so release should return False. I ran this with an already-expired lease and release returned True.
issues.example: m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=-1); m.acquire('r','a'); m.release('r','a') returns True
issues.fix: Before deleting, check `datetime.datetime.utcnow() >= lock_info['expires_at']`. If the lease has expired, remove the stale entry if you like and return False.
issues.test_code:
m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=-1)
assert m.acquire('r','a')
res = m.release('r','a')
assert res is False, res

issues.title: Deprecated naive utcnow() used for lease timing
issues.explanation: `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated and returns naive datetimes. A monotonic clock, or timezone-aware time, would be more robust for lease timing. A monotonic clock is not affected by wall-clock adjustments. The code assumes the system clock never jumps.
issues.fix: Use time.monotonic() or datetime.now(timezone.utc).

issues.title: release succeeds for an expired lease
issues.explanation: The contract says release unlocks only if the requesting owner holds the active lock. release never checks `expires_at`. An owner whose lease has expired therefore gets True and the entry is deleted, even though they no longer hold an active lock. With a lease of 0 seconds, the lock is already expired when acquire returns, yet release returns True.
issues.example: m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=0); m.acquire('r','a'); m.release('r','a') returns True
issues.fix: In release, compare `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` with `lock_info['expires_at']`. If the lease has expired, return False (optionally deleting the stale entry first).
issues.test_code:
m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=0)
assert m.acquire('r','a') is True
r = m.release('r','a')
assert r is False, r

issues.title: Deprecated naive utcnow() used for lease timing
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns naive datetimes. The wall clock can also jump, which would shorten or extend leases. time.monotonic() or timezone-aware datetimes would be more robust. The class also assumes single-threaded use, so there is no locking around the check-then-set in acquire.
issues.fix: Use time.monotonic() or datetime.now(timezone.utc). Add a threading.Lock if the class is used from several threads.

critic.title: release succeeds for an expired lease
critic.reason: The contract says release succeeds only for the holder of an active lock, and release never checks expires_at, so an expired owner gets True. The test shows this. The 'optionally' covers only deleting the stale entry, which the contract does not require, so the required part of the fix is not hedged.

issues.title: release succeeds on an expired lease
issues.explanation: The docstring says release unlocks only if the requesting owner holds the active lock. release never checks `expires_at`. An owner whose lease has expired still gets True and deletes the entry, so it reports a successful release of a lock it no longer holds. Because release returns False when no lock exists, the result is also inconsistent: the same call returns True or False depending on whether the expired entry has been replaced.
issues.example: m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=0); m.acquire('r','a'); m.release('r','a') returns True, but the lease has already expired.
issues.fix: In release, compare `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` with `lock_info['expires_at']`. If the lease has expired, drop the stale entry if you want, and return False.

issues.title: Deprecated naive utcnow and unbounded stale entries
issues.explanation: `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated and returns a naive datetime. Expired entries are only replaced when the same resource is acquired again, so entries for resources that are never reacquired stay in the dict. This assumes the set of resource ids is small.
issues.fix: Use `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` or `time.monotonic()`. Optionally purge expired entries.

issues.title: Deprecated naive utcnow() used as the clock
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns naive datetimes. It follows the wall clock, so NTP adjustments or clock changes can stall or distort refill. This assumes the wall clock never jumps. time.monotonic() would be a better fit for measuring elapsed time.
issues.fix: Use time.monotonic() and store floats, or at least datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).

issues.title: Bucket dictionary grows without bound
issues.explanation: Each distinct key adds an entry to _buckets that is never evicted, even after the bucket has refilled to full capacity. With many distinct keys, such as client IPs, memory grows without limit. This assumes a bounded key space.
issues.fix: Evict entries that have fully refilled, or drop stale keys periodically.

issues.title: Bucket dictionary grows without bound
issues.explanation: Every distinct key adds an entry to `_buckets`, and entries are never evicted, even after they have refilled to full capacity. With many distinct keys, such as client IPs, memory grows without limit. A bucket that is full is equivalent to a missing one, so it could be dropped. The class also assumes single-threaded use. The read-modify-write in `consume` is not atomic, so concurrent callers could both pass the check.
issues.fix: Periodically evict entries that have refilled to capacity, or add a TTL or max-size cap. Guard `consume` with a lock if threads are used.

issues.title: Deprecated naive utcnow() used and the clock cannot be injected
issues.explanation: `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime. The wall clock can also jump backwards. This makes the limiter hard to test deterministically. The code assumes the clock is monotonic. A backward jump freezes refill until time catches up.
issues.fix: Use `time.monotonic()`, or accept an injectable clock function.

issues.title: consume lacks a docstring and silently approves non-positive requests
issues.explanation: `consume` returns True for `tokens_to_consume <= 0` without recording anything. Neither the docstring nor the code explains this. Requests larger than the capacity can never succeed, and that is not documented either.
issues.fix: Document these behaviors, or raise ValueError for non-positive counts.

issues.title: Bucket dictionary grows without bound
issues.explanation: Every distinct key adds an entry to `_buckets`, and nothing ever removes it. A long-running service that rate-limits by IP or user id will use more and more memory. Entries for keys that have fully refilled could be dropped, because a missing key already means a full bucket.
issues.fix: Periodically evict buckets that have refilled to capacity, or store an expiry time and prune expired entries.

issues.title: Uses deprecated, naive wall-clock `utcnow()` for interval timing
issues.explanation: `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime. It is also a wall clock, so NTP adjustments can make elapsed time wrong. The code assumes the clock never goes backwards. A monotonic clock such as `time.monotonic()` fits this use better. The clock is also hard-coded, which makes the class hard to test.
issues.fix: Use `time.monotonic()`, or inject a clock function into the constructor.

issues.title: Non-positive token requests silently succeed, and the class is not thread-safe
issues.explanation: `consume` returns True for `tokens_to_consume <= 0` without validating it, so a negative or zero request is always allowed. The read-modify-write on `_buckets` has no lock, so it assumes a single thread. Neither point is stated in the docstring.
issues.fix: Raise `ValueError` for non-positive requests, or document that they are allowed. Add a lock if the limiter is used from several threads.

issues.title: get_session_metadata returns the whole session record, not the metadata
issues.explanation: The name says it returns the session's metadata. It returns the full session dict, which holds the token, the metadata and created_at. A caller expecting only the metadata gets the wrong structure. It also exposes the session token to any caller that only wanted metadata.
issues.example: m = UserSessionManager(); m.create_or_update_session('u1', {'ip': '1.2.3.4'}); m.get_session_metadata('u1') returns {'token':..., 'metadata':{...}, 'created_at':...}
issues.fix: Return the stored metadata: `session = self.active_sessions.get(user_id); return session["metadata"] if session else None`.
issues.test_code:
m = UserSessionManager()
m.create_or_update_session('u1', {'ip': '1.2.3.4'})
r = m.get_session_metadata('u1')
assert r == {'ip': '1.2.3.4'}, r
assert m.get_session_metadata('nobody') is None

issues.title: Session token is predictable
issues.explanation: The token is built from the user_id and a one-second timestamp, and both are easy to guess. An attacker can forge a valid token for any user. Two calls for the same user in the same second also return the same token.
issues.example: create_or_update_session('alice', {}) returns 'tok_alice_1700000000'. This can be guessed by trying nearby timestamps.
issues.fix: Use `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` for the token. Keep a separate mapping from token to user if you need lookup by token.

issues.title: Naive utcnow().timestamp() and deprecated utcnow
issues.explanation: This code assumes the server's local timezone is UTC. `datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive datetime, and `.timestamp()` interprets it as local time, so the value is wrong on any other timezone. `utcnow` is also deprecated. The same call is made twice (lines 9 and 13), so the two timestamps can differ.
issues.fix: Call `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` once and reuse the value.

issues.title: get_session_metadata returns the whole session record, not the metadata
issues.explanation: The method name says it returns the session's metadata. It returns the full internal record, which has the keys token, metadata and created_at. Callers get the wrong structure. The session token is also exposed to anything that only asked for metadata.

issues.fix: Return the stored metadata: `s = self.active_sessions.get(user_id); return s['metadata'] if s else None`.

issues.explanation: The token is built from the user id and a timestamp in seconds, so anyone who knows a user id and roughly when they logged in can guess it. It is not random. Calling the method twice for the same user in the same second also produces the same token.
issues.example: create_or_update_session('alice', {}) returns 'tok_alice_<epoch seconds>'
issues.fix: Use `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` to generate the token.

issues.title: Naive utcnow().timestamp() is interpreted as local time
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns a naive datetime. Calling .timestamp() on it treats it as local time, so the value is wrong on any machine that isn't set to UTC. Line 13 calls utcnow() a second time, so the token time and created_at can differ.
issues.fix: Use `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` once and reuse it for both the token and created_at.

issues.title: get_session_metadata returns the whole session record instead of only the metadata
issues.explanation: You confirmed the method should return only the metadata dict that was passed to create_or_update_session. It returns the full record, which also holds the token and created_at. This leaks the session token to callers and returns the wrong shape.

issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() returns a naive datetime. Calling .timestamp() on it treats it as local time, so the number is wrong when the machine is not set to UTC. utcnow() is also deprecated. The token is the user id plus whole seconds, so two updates within the same second give the same token. This assumes tokens only need to identify a session. You said there is no requirement for unguessable tokens, so I am not reporting it as a security bug.
